beats.intro: Chapter one, lesson three. Chemical and nutritional classification. [[shelf]]Picture a supermarket shelf: eggs, milk, beans, rice. Every one of these foods is full of protein, and every protein is a chain of amino acids. [[card]]Here is our amino acid card from lesson one, with its four tabs. [[tabs]]Today we light up two of them. The chemical tab sorts amino acids by their charge. The nutritional tab sorts them by whether we must eat them.
beats.count: [[rule]]Start with the chemical classification. The rule is simple: count the groups. Every amino acid has an amino group and a carboxyl group on its alpha carbon. But some have a second one hiding in the side chain. [[ala]]Take alanine. One amino group, one carboxyl group. One and one: the counts are equal, so the amino acid is neutral. [[twelve]]Neutral is the biggest class. The slide lists twelve: glycine, alanine, serine, threonine, cysteine, cystine, valine, leucine, isoleucine, phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan. [[cystine]]A small note: cystine is two cysteines joined by a disulfide bridge, so it is really the oxidized form of cysteine. [[more]]Two more neutral ones, methionine and proline, are missing from the slide's list. They have one of each too.
beats.acid: [[asp]]Now aspartic acid. Its alpha carbon has the usual amino group and carboxyl group. But look at the side chain: it ends in a second carboxyl group. So we count one amino group, and two carboxyl groups. [[acid]]Carboxyl groups outnumber amino groups, so the amino acid is acidic. [[minus]]And there is a charge. At body pH, a carboxyl group gives away its hydrogen and turns negative. Extra carboxyl groups mean extra negative charge, so the acidic amino acids carry a negative charge. [[glu]]There are two: aspartic acid, and glutamic acid, which is the same idea with a longer side chain.
beats.basic: [[lys]]Next, lysine. One carboxyl group, but two amino groups: one on the alpha carbon, and one at the far end of its long side chain. [[basic]]Amino groups outnumber carboxyl groups, so lysine is basic. [[plus]]At body pH, an amino group picks up a hydrogen and turns positive. Extra amino groups mean extra positive charge, so the basic amino acids carry a positive charge. [[ahl]]There are three, and the slide's memory trick is A, H, L: arginine, histidine, lysine. [[ring]]Arginine and histidine keep their extra basic nitrogen in the side chain too, in a guanidino group and in a ring. So count it as an extra basic group, not always a plain amino group. [[two]]And histidine wears two labels: heterocyclic by the shape of its side chain, and basic by its charge. Two schemes, both right.
beats.q1: Quick check. Lysine has two amino groups and one carboxyl group. Which chemical class is it?
beats.sort: [[bins]]Let's sort. Three bins: neutral, acidic, basic. [[n]]Equal counts go to neutral. [[a]]More carboxyl groups: acidic, negative. [[b]]More amino groups: basic, positive. [[tip]]A tip to remember it: an acid gives away hydrogen, so it ends up negative. A base takes hydrogen, so it ends up positive.
beats.diet: [[diet]]Now the nutritional tab. Your body can build many amino acids from other molecules. But not all of them. [[ess]]Essential amino acids are not synthesized in the body. They must come in the diet, from eggs, milk, meat and beans. [[non]]Non-essential amino acids are synthesized in the body, so you do not have to eat them. Careful with the words: non-essential does not mean unimportant. Your body needs them. It just makes them itself. [[miss]]If an essential one is missing from the diet, the body cannot make up for it, and protein building stalls.
beats.mnem: [[tvm]]The slide gives a memory trick for the essential amino acids: Try, This, V I P, Mall. [[try]]Try: tryptophan. [[this]]This: threonine and histidine. [[vip]]V I P: valine, isoleucine and phenylalanine. [[mall]]Mall: methionine, arginine, leucine and lysine. [[ten]]That is ten names. Say the trick aloud, and walk down the shelf.
beats.semi: [[semi]]Look closely: two of those ten, arginine and histidine, are semi-essential. [[kids]]Growing children need them in food, because a growing body cannot make enough. Adults can make enough, so for adults they are not essential. [[eight]]So the strict essentials, needed by everyone, are the other eight.
beats.q2: Quick check. Which of these four can the body make for itself: leucine, glycine, lysine or tryptophan?
beats.rest: [[rest]]Everything else is non-essential: glycine, alanine, serine, tyrosine, cysteine, cystine, aspartic acid, glutamic acid and proline. [[tyr]]Notice tyrosine. It looks a lot like phenylalanine, but the body makes tyrosine from phenylalanine. So phenylalanine is essential, and tyrosine is not. [[two2]]Two more of the twenty, asparagine and glutamine, are not on the slide's lists. They are also made in the body. [[food]]And foods? Egg, milk and meat carry all the essential ones. A plant food may be short of one or two, so a mix, like rice with beans, covers the gaps.
beats.wrap: [[w1]]Let's put it together on the card. Chemical: count the groups. Equal is neutral. More carboxyl is acidic, and negative. More amino is basic, and positive. [[w2]]Nutritional: ten essential, from the diet: Try, This, V I P, Mall. [[w3]]Arginine and histidine are semi-essential, needed by growing children. The rest, the body makes. [[w4]]One amino acid, two labels: lysine is basic and essential. Glutamic acid is acidic and non-essential.
